{
  "winner": "B",
  "reasons": [
    "B's brief shows people already pay for the exact feature. Maskwire sells 'Alias replies' as a named tool in a $3/month bundle, and addy.io and SimpleLogin include it in paid tiers. A's only paid anchor is ReviewGuard's $1.99/month Pro tier, which covers Google Maps and TripAdvisor reviews, not the Reddit bot-filtering use case. A's direct Reddit competitors (SlopSieve, Redd-Eye) are all free.",
    "B's demand evidence names a concrete, recurring problem: replies going out from the wrong From address. It is documented across four mail-client forums (Zoho, Apple, Microsoft, eM Client) over several years. A's demand quotes express general annoyance with bots but never ask for a tool or a fix.",
    "B's core logic is deterministic: map the recipient header to the From address. The product either works or it doesn't. A depends on noisy AI-detection heuristics, and its own brief says false positives could harm the core use case by misflagging real users.",
    "A also depends on the page structure and terms of service of third-party sites it doesn't control. B's main operational risk is GDPR obligations if it proxies email. A plugin-based build reduces that risk, and the brief already plans a one-time legal consult to address it.",
    "Both ideas face crowded markets. A's case against is stronger: at least four free, maintained, similarly scoped competitors, and no evidence that anyone pays in the Reddit niche."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "A's demand evidence does not show anyone wants a tool for this, let alone would pay. It consists of two Reddit comments complaining about bots (one says the user took time away from Reddit) and a secondhand Slashdot summary of the Reddit CEO's remarks. These show the problem exists. None of them shows interest in a filtering extension or willingness to pay, which matters most when free alternatives already exist.",
  "confidence_note": "Low confidence. Both ideas are commodity products in markets saturated with free or bundled incumbents, and neither brief offers direct evidence that anyone would pay for a standalone version. B wins narrowly because its brief shows paid demand for the feature and a deterministic product. There is a caveat: several of B's forum quotes come from business users with role addresses (info@, admin), not the privacy-conscious prosumers named as payers. B's incumbents may also absorb most willingness to pay, and a free Thunderbird extension already covers the client-side case."
}
